graders.evidence:
## What a Bloom filter is, and when it pays off

A Bloom filter is a small, fixed-size structure that answers one question about a set of keys: has this key been added? It is built from an array of bits, all zero at the start, and k hash functions. Putting it in front of a slow lookup lets most queries for missing keys end without running the lookup.

Adding a key runs it through the k hash functions and sets the k bits they point to. Checking a key runs the same hashes and reads those k bits. If any bit is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set that bit. If all are 1, the key probably was added. The word "probably" is needed because bits are shared. Other keys may have set all k of them, and the filter then reports a key it never saw. This is a false positive. A false negative cannot happen, since a key that was added keeps its bits set.

The false positive rate depends on how full the array is, because every added key sets more bits and a check on an absent key is more likely to find all k of its bits already set. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hashes the rate is near 1%. For a given array size and key count, the best number of hashes is bits per key times ln 2, which is about 7 at 10 bits per key. Computing k separate hashes per key is not needed in practice: double hashing derives all k bit positions from two hash values, so the filter needs two real hash functions.

What the filter gives up follows from how it stores keys. It holds no keys and no values, so it cannot list its contents or return the value for a key. It cannot remove a key either, because clearing one of that key's bits could clear a bit another key depends on, and that key would then become a false negative. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, incremented on add and decremented on removal, so that keys can be deleted, at the cost of more space per slot.

These properties decide when a filter is worth adding. A "no" is certain and a "yes" still has to be confirmed by the real lookup, so the filter saves work on the queries whose answer is no. It suits a lookup that is slow and is often asked about keys that are absent, where the lookup keeps its own copy of the keys and values and the filter only screens it.

LevelDB uses it this way. It keeps one filter per file on disk, and a read checks each file's filter before touching the file. Every file whose filter says no is skipped, and at a 1% false positive rate a file that does not hold the key is read unnecessarily about once in a hundred checks.

## What a Bloom filter is, and when it pays off

A Bloom filter is a fixed-size structure that tells you whether a key is in a set, cheaply enough to sit in front of a slow lookup. The lookup then runs for the keys the filter cannot rule out.

Checking a key hashes it the same way and reads those k bits. If any of them is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set all of them. If all are 1, the key probably was added. Double hashing derives all k positions from two hash values, so two hash functions are enough to supply any k.

The answer is "probably" because bits are shared. Other keys may have set the same k bits, so a key that was never added can find them all at 1, which is a false positive. A key that was added always finds its bits set, so the filter never gives a false negative. As the array fills, more bits are 1 and false positives become more common. A filter holds no keys and no values, so it cannot list what it contains or return anything stored under a key.

A "no" from the filter is certain, and the slow lookup is skipped. A "yes" means the lookup runs, and a false positive is a lookup that finds nothing. The filter therefore pays off when most lookups are for absent keys and the only thing needed from the filter is a verdict on whether to look. When most keys are present, the filter says yes nearly every time and saves little.

LevelDB uses it this way. It keeps one filter per file on disk, and a read skips every file whose filter says no.

## What a Bloom filter is, and when it is worth using

A Bloom filter is a small, fixed-size structure that answers one question about a set of keys: has this key been added? It is kept in front of a slow lookup, such as a read from disk, so that the lookup only runs for keys that might be present.

The filter is an array of bits, all 0 at the start, together with k hash functions. Adding a key runs it through each hash function and sets the k bits that the hashes point to. Checking a key computes the same k positions and reads those bits. If any of them is 0, the key was never added, because adding it would have set all k. If all of them are 1, the key probably was added.

The answer is "probably" because other keys can set the same bits. A key that was never added may find every one of its k positions already set by keys that were, and the filter then reports a false positive. A false negative cannot happen, since a bit that was set is never cleared. The false positive rate rises as the array fills, so it depends on how many bits the filter has per key. With about 10 bits per key and 7 hash functions the rate is near 1%. For a given array size and key count, the best number of hash functions is bits per key times ln 2, which is where 7 comes from at 10 bits per key. Computing k independent hashes per key is costly, so implementations derive all k positions from two real hash values by double hashing.

This gives the rule for when a filter pays off. A "no" is certain, so the slow lookup is skipped. A "yes" still has to be confirmed by the lookup, and a false positive costs one lookup that finds nothing. The filter therefore helps when many of the lookups are for keys that are absent, and it helps more the cheaper the check is compared with the lookup it replaces. LevelDB is the standard case. It keeps one filter for each file on disk, and a read consults the filters first and skips every file whose filter says no, so it opens only the few files that might hold the key.

The filter holds only bits, which limits what it can do. It cannot remove a key, because clearing a bit could erase another key that shares it. A counting variant replaces each bit with a small counter, incrementing on add and decrementing on remove, so keys can be deleted at the cost of more space per slot. No variant can list the keys it holds or return a value for one, so the filter can only decide whether to do the lookup and never replaces it.

Write the explainer section for a Go language guide, for a developer about to use defer to release resources. The question it answers: When does a deferred call run in Go, for someone using defer to release a resource?

Facts, each checked against the Go specification:

- `defer` schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, not at the end of the enclosing block.
- The arguments of the deferred call are evaluated when the `defer` statement runs, not when the call runs.
- For a method call, the receiver is evaluated when the `defer` statement runs too.
- Deferred calls run last in, first out.
- Deferred calls also run when the function panics.
- A deferred function literal can read and set the function's named results.
- In a loop each iteration adds a deferred call, and none run until the function returns, so `defer f.Close()` in a loop keeps every file open until then.
- A deferred call of a nil function value panics when the call runs, not at the `defer` statement.
- Since Go 1.14 the compiler inlines most defers at function exit, so a defer costs a few nanoseconds.

## When a deferred call runs

A deferred call is a function call that Go postpones until the surrounding function returns. It exists so that the line that releases a resource can sit directly under the line that acquires it, and still run on every path out of the function.

The call runs when the function returns, whatever block the `defer` statement sits in. A `defer` inside an `if` or `for` body waits for the whole function, not for the end of that body. It also runs when the function panics, so a file is closed or a lock released while the panic unwinds. When a function defers several calls they run last in, first out, which releases resources in the reverse of the order they were acquired.

The call is postponed, but its operands are not. When the `defer` statement executes, Go evaluates the function value and the arguments, and saves them for later. In the following code the deferred call prints 1, because `x` was read when the statement ran:

```go
x := 1
defer fmt.Println(x)
x = 2
```

For a method call the receiver is evaluated at the same moment. In `defer f.Close()` the file that gets closed is the one `f` held at the `defer` statement, even if `f` is assigned a different file afterwards.

A loop adds one deferred call per iteration, and none of them runs until the function returns. A function that opens a file in each iteration and writes `defer f.Close()` therefore keeps every file open until it finishes. Moving the loop body into a helper function gives each iteration its own return, and so its own deferred call.

A deferred function literal can also read and set the function's named results. Because it runs after the `return` statement has assigned them, it can report an error that only appears at release time, such as a failed `Close` after a write:

```go
func write(name string, data []byte) (err error) {
	f, err := os.Create(name)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer func() {
		if cerr := f.Close(); err == nil {
			err = cerr
		}
	}()
	_, err = f.Write(data)
	return err
}
```

A deferred call is a function call that Go postpones until the surrounding function returns. It lets the code that releases a resource sit next to the code that acquired it, and it runs when the function returns or panics.

```go
f, err := os.Open(name)
if err != nil {

}
defer f.Close()
```

It also runs when the function panics, so a deferred Close or Unlock happens while the panic unwinds. When a function defers several calls, they run last in, first out, which releases resources in the reverse of the order they were acquired.

A return statement sets the function's results first and then the deferred calls run, so a literal can read and set the named results. That lets it replace the returned error with one that records a failed Close.

Each iteration of a loop adds another deferred call, and none of them run until the function returns. With `defer f.Close()` in a loop over file names, every file stays open until the function returns, which can exhaust the process's file descriptors. Moving the loop body into its own function closes each file when that function returns.

A deferred call of a nil function value panics when the call runs, so the panic comes at function return and the defer statement succeeds. Since Go 1.14 the compiler inlines most defers at function exit, and a defer in ordinary code costs a few nanoseconds.

Write the explainer section for the groupcache README, for a developer deciding whether to use groupcache. The question it answers: How does groupcache work, for someone deciding whether to use it?

- The hot cache is bounded relative to the main cache, so copies of peer-owned keys cannot take over the keys the process owns.
- When a peer joins or leaves, only the keys on its part of the ring change owner.
- Singleflight allows one in-flight load per key. A million `Get("FOO")` calls run the `Getter` once.
- If the owner is unreachable, the asking process runs the `Getter` itself, so the `Getter` can run on more than one process.
- `Set()`, `Remove()` and `RemoveKeys()` go to the owner and then to every other peer, best effort, so values should carry an expiry.
- The default cache is an LRU. The Otter cache uses lock-free S3-FIFO eviction.
- HTTP is the default transport.
- Stats are OpenTelemetry metrics.
- There is no global state.

groupcache is a Go library for caching across a cluster of processes. Every process holds part of the cache and serves it to the others, so the cluster has no cache servers to run. Each process is told who its peers are through `SetPeers()`.

cases.name: writing-prose-write-ahead-log
cases.promptMarkdown:
Write the explainer section for a database internals guide, for a developer who has not seen how databases survive a crash. The question it answers: How does a write-ahead log keep a database from losing committed data in a crash?

Facts, each checked against the Postgres documentation:

- A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change.
- The database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later.
- Before it changes a page, it appends a record describing the change to the log.
- A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync. The data pages do not have to be.
- Appending to the end of a file is sequential, so flushing the log costs much less than flushing pages scattered across the data files.
- After a crash the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page.
- Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it, so replay skips records a page already has.
- A checkpoint writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. The log before it can be deleted or reused.
- Postgres calls this the WAL, and replicas stay current by replaying the same records.
- Postgres stores the log in 16 MB segment files by default.
- In Postgres an LSN is a byte position in the log.

## How a write-ahead log survives a crash

A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change. A database changes data pages in memory and writes them to disk later, so at any moment some committed work exists only in memory, and a crash would erase it. The log keeps a copy of that work on disk.

Before the database changes a page, it appends a record describing the change to the log. A transaction commits when its records and a commit record have been flushed to disk with fsync. The data pages do not have to be flushed. When fsync returns, everything needed to redo the transaction is on disk, and the database can tell the client the commit succeeded. This is also cheap, because appending to the end of a file is sequential, and flushing the log costs much less than flushing pages scattered across the data files.

After a crash, memory is gone and the data files are missing some committed changes. The database replays the log from the last checkpoint and reapplies each record to its page. Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it. During replay the database compares the two and skips a record the page already has. Some pages reached disk before the crash and some did not, and replay brings both kinds to the same final state.

A checkpoint is what limits how much of the log replay has to read. It writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. Everything before that position is already in the data files, so recovery starts there, and the log before it can be deleted or reused.

Postgres calls this log the WAL and stores it in 16 MB segment files by default. An LSN in Postgres is a byte position in the log. Replicas stay current by replaying the same records that crash recovery would.

## How a write-ahead log survives a crash

A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it makes the change. Flushing the log is also cheap. Appending to the end of a file is sequential, so a commit costs much less than it would if the database had to flush pages scattered across the data files.

Recovery starts from the last checkpoint. The database replays the log from there and reapplies each record to its page. Every record has a log sequence number (LSN), and every page stores the LSN of the last record applied to it. Replay compares the two and skips any record the page already has, which covers pages that reached disk before the crash.

A checkpoint writes all modified pages to disk and notes the log position. Everything in the log before that position describes changes already on disk, so it can be deleted or reused, and replay only has to cover the log written since.

Postgres calls this log the WAL and stores it in 16 MB segment files by default. An LSN in Postgres is a byte position in the log. Replicas stay current by replaying the same records that crash recovery would.
